title: Bài sưu tầm 123 - Passage 1: Maria Sibylla Merian: Pioneer of Insect Illustration
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 1 — TEST 123

Maria Sibylla Merian: Pioneer of Insect Illustration

Paragraph 1. Born in Frankfurt in 1647, Maria Sibylla Merian grew up inside a busy publishing and artistic household. Following her father's early death, she was trained by her stepfather, Jacob Marrel, a painter known for lucrative still-life compositions of flowers. Although Marrel encouraged her to concentrate on commercially popular botanical themes and regarded creeping insects merely as blemishes on petals, the young girl became fascinated by the caterpillars hiding in his studio garden. At thirteen, she began raising silkworms, filling thick notebooks with dated observations and watercolour studies tracing every stage from egg to moth.

Paragraph 2. At that time, European science knew remarkably little about insect development. Most naturalists still assumed that insects emerged spontaneously out of decaying mud or rotting meat, rather than hatching from eggs laid by adults. By breeding hundreds of local caterpillars in glass jars, Merian proved that each species followed a precise, predictable metamorphosis. In 1679, she published her first illustrated book on European caterpillars in German rather than scholarly Latin, selling copies directly to collectors to finance her studio. Even more unusually, instead of drawing dead, pinned insects against blank white pages, she portrayed living creatures perched on the exact plants they relied upon for food.

Paragraph 3. Merian's curiosity deepened after she moved to Amsterdam in 1691 and inspected dried tropical butterflies brought back from Dutch colonies. Realizing that preserved specimens revealed nothing about living habits or larval diets, she took an extraordinary step for a woman of her era. In 1699, at the age of fifty-two, she sold many of her own paintings to pay for a transatlantic voyage and sailed for the Dutch colony of Surinam with her younger daughter, Dorothea. Hoping to spend five full years documenting jungle species, the pair set up a base in Paramaribo and ventured into coastal forests with the assistance of enslaved local guides who knew where rare larvae fed.

Paragraph 4. Fieldwork in the humid tropics proved physically punishing. Weakened by a persistent tropical fever, Merian was forced to cut her expedition short after just twenty-one months and return to Amsterdam. Back in the Netherlands, she spent four years turning her field sketches into sixty large copperplate engravings. Published in 1705, Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium astonished European scholars with vivid depictions of tarantulas, army ants, and giant moths interacting in their native habitats.

Paragraph 5. Despite early admiration, Merian's scientific standing faded after her death in 1717. Nineteenth-century male commentators belittled her volumes as mere decoration for wealthy drawing rooms, even questioning whether a bird-eating spider really existed. Modern biologists, however, have thoroughly vindicated her accuracy, praising her as a founder of ecological illustration for showing how insects and vegetation depend on one another decades before ecology became an academic field.

groups.title: Questions 8–13
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 123?
In boxes 8–13 on your answer sheet, write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 1: "filling thick notebooks with dated observations and watercolour studies".
Đoạn 2: "emerged spontaneously out of decaying mud or rotting meat".
Đoạn 2: "portrayed living creatures perched on the exact plants they relied upon for food".
Đoạn 3: "sailed for the Dutch colony of Surinam with her younger daughter, Dorothea".
Đoạn 4: "Weakened by a persistent tropical fever, Merian was forced to cut her expedition short".
Đoạn 5: "belittled her volumes as mere decoration for wealthy drawing rooms".

q8.text: Merian's stepfather encouraged her to focus exclusively on drawing insects rather than botanical subjects.

steps: Đoạn 1: Bố dượng muốn bà tập trung vẽ chủ đề thực vật (hoa) bán chạy và coi côn trùng chỉ là vết bẩn trên cánh hoa (encouraged her to concentrate on commercially popular botanical themes).

q9.text: Several European royal courts purchased copies of her 1679 caterpillar book.

steps: Đoạn 2: Bài nói bà xuất bản sách bằng tiếng Đức năm 1679 và bán cho các nhà sưu tầm, nhưng không nhắc đến việc triều đình hoàng gia châu Âu có mua hay không.

q10.text: Most seventeenth-century experts misunderstood how insects came into existence.

steps: Đoạn 2: Hầu hết nhà tự nhiên học thời đó tin côn trùng tự sinh ra từ bùn thối hay thịt ôi chứ không phải nở từ trứng.

q11.text: Merian completed the full five-year fieldwork schedule she had originally planned in Surinam.

steps: Đoạn 3 & 4: Bà dự định ở 5 năm (five full years), nhưng bị sốt nhiệt đới buộc phải cắt ngắn chuyến đi chỉ sau 21 tháng (twenty-one months).

q12.text: Dorothea remained in South America for several months after her mother departed for Europe.

steps: Đoạn 4: Bài chỉ nêu Merian phải về Amsterdam sớm sau 21 tháng vì sốt, không nói rõ Dorothea về cùng lúc hay ở lại thêm.

q13.text: Modern scientists value Merian's drawings for showing how organisms interact with their environment.

steps: Đoạn 5: Các nhà sinh học hiện đại ca ngợi bà là người tiên phong minh họa sinh thái vì đã thể hiện mối liên hệ phụ thuộc giữa côn trùng và thực vật.
